claim: Shigella flexneri are pathogenic bacteria belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family, and infection in humans causes diarrhea and severe inflammation in the gut.
source: Shigella flexneri are pathogenic bacteria belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family, and infection in humans causes diarrhea and severe inflammation in the gut.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Shigella flexneri pathogenicity.

claim: Upon entry into the cytoplasm of infected cells, a sub-population of Shigella bacteria hijacks the actin cytoskeleton and stimulates its polymerization on the bacterial surface, forming actin comet tails.
source: Upon entry into the cytoplasm of infected cells, a sub-population of the bacteria hijacks the actin cytoskeleton and stimulates its polymerization on the bacterial surface, forming so-called actin comet tails (Ray et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ray et al., 2009.

claim: Shigella bacteria propel rapidly through the cytoplasm reaching speeds of up to 0.5 µm/s.
source: allowing them to propel rapidly through the cytoplasm reaching speeds of up to 0.5 µm/s (Gouin et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gouin et al., 1999.

claim: Bacteria oftentimes collided with mitochondria, pushing the mitochondrial tubules aside, above or below.
source: Using time-lapse microscopy, we observed that bacteria oftentimes collided with mitochondria, pushing the mitochondrial tubules aside, above or below (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: Observed through time-lapse microscopy experiments and shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: In 60% of cases where collisions caused visible reduction of mitochondrial fluorescence, mitochondria underwent fission at the constricted site within one to five minutes.
source: In 60% of such cases, mitochondria underwent fission at the constricted site within one to five minutes (n = 23; Figure 1B and Video 2).
evidence: Quantified from experimental observations with n=23 events, shown in Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: Merely 4% of non-stimulated mitochondria underwent fission within a five-minute time span.
source: By contrast, we observed that merely 4% of non-stimulated mitochondria underwent fission within a five-minute time span.
evidence: Quantified from control observations in the study.

claim: DRP1 is necessary for bacteria-induced fission.
source: These results indicate that DRP1 is necessary for bacteria-induced fission.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that DRP1 depletion completely abolished motile Shigella-induced fission.

claim: Mitochondria from DRP1CRISPR cells recovered without undergoing fission in 100% of the cases (n = 50) after bacterial collision.
source: However, in contrast to wild-type cells, mitochondria from DRP1CRISPR cells recovered without undergoing fission in 100% of the cases (n = 50, Figure 1C, Video 3, p<10−7 from a Fisher's exact test)
evidence: Quantified from experimental observations with n=50 events, shown in Figure 1C and Video 3, with statistical significance p<10^-7.

claim: DRP1 siRNA treatment completely abolished motile Shigella-induced fission in wild-type cells (n = 19, p<10−4).
source: Similarly, DRP1 siRNA treatment completely abolished motile Shigella-induced fission in wild-type cells (n = 19, p<10−4).
evidence: Quantified from experimental observations with n=19 events and statistical significance p<10^-4.

claim: DRP1 foci formation was observed at sites where motile bacteria had crossed a mitochondrial tubule, and these sites subsequently underwent fission.
source: Upon Shigella infection, we observed DRP1 foci formation at sites where motile bacteria had crossed a mitochondrial tubule. These sites subsequently underwent fission (Figure 1D, Video 4).
evidence: Observed in experiments with mCherry-tagged DRP1, shown in Figure 1D and Video 4.

claim: Mitochondria react to collisions with bacteria by actively undergoing fission.
source: Together with DRP1 depletion data, these results indicate that mitochondria react to collisions with bacteria by actively undergoing fission.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including DRP1 recruitment and depletion studies.

claim: Adherent cells have a very flat periphery (typically 100–200 nm thick).
source: Adherent cells have a very flat periphery (typically 100–200 nm thick [Xu et al., 2012])
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2012.

claim: 36 of 41 successful AFM approaches led to mitochondrial fission.
source: 36 of 41 successful approaches led to fission (success being scored as inducing a visible constriction of the mitochondrial matrix. All fission events were scored within 5 min).
evidence: Quantified from AFM experiments with defined success criteria.

claim: AFM stimulation in DRP1-deficient cells led to a significant decrease in fission events upon force application (10 fission events in 41 attempts, p<10−8).
source: Indeed, these events were again DRP1-dependent, since repeating these experiments in DRP1-deficient cells led to a significant decrease in fission events upon force application (10 fission events in 41 attempts, p<10−8; Figure 2B,D, Video 7).
evidence: Quantified from AFM experiments in DRP1-deficient cells with statistical significance p<10^-8, shown in Figure 2B,D and Video 7.

claim: Forces in the nanonewton range are typically needed to induce deformation of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Of note, forces in the nanonewton range are typically needed to induce deformation of the actin cytoskeleton (Hadjiantoniou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hadjiantoniou et al., 2012.

claim: The surface of gramophone records consists of grooves 40 µm deep and 80 µm wide approximately, and flat ledges between the grooves.
source: The surface of gramophone records consists of grooves 40 µm deep and 80 µm wide approximately, and flat ledges between the grooves (Read, 1952) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Read, 1952 and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When grown on vinyl records, the spreading of the cell across the ledge over into the groove causes the peripheral cytoplasmic content to be constricted along the edge.
source: We hypothesized that, when grown on vinyl records, the spreading of the cell across the ledge over into the groove would cause the peripheral cytoplasmic content to be constricted along the edge. To verify this, we imaged cells expressing an ER marker – GFP-Sec61β – as a proxy for the cytoplasm (Kanfer et al., 2015). Indeed, as shown in Figure 3B and Video 9, 3D-reconstruction of a cell spreading over the edge shows that the cytoplasm is constricted right over the edge.
evidence: Verified through imaging experiments shown in Figure 3B and Video 9.

claim: The cytoplasmic areas of cells spanning the edge of the groove were usually devoid of mitochondria.
source: Indeed, the cytoplasmic areas of cells spanning the edge of the groove were usually devoid of mitochondria (Figure 3C scrambled siRNA and wild-type).
evidence: Observed in experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mitochondria vacated the edge area by first undergoing fission (averagely within 93 s), and then moving towards the ledge and the groove areas.
source: Indeed, a few minutes into time-lapse recording, mitochondria vacated the edge area by first undergoing fission (averagely within 93 s), and then moving towards the ledge and the groove areas (Figure 3E and Video 10).
evidence: Observed through time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 3E and Video 10.

claim: A complete division of the mitochondrial network along the edge of the groove was observed in ~80% of wild-type cells, but only in 15% and 43% of the DRP1 siRNA-treated and DRP1CRISPR knockout cells, respectively.
source: We observed a complete division of the mitochondrial network along the edge of the groove in ~80% of wild-type cells, but only in 15% and 43% of the DRP1 siRNA-treated and DRP1CRISPR knockout cells, respectively (Figure 3D, p<10−16 and p<10−9, from a Fisher's exact test)
evidence: Quantified from experiments shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance p<10^-16 and p<10^-9.

claim: Mitochondria undergo DRP1-mediated fission in constricted cytoplasmic regions caused by cell adhesion to uneven surfaces.
source: Thus, mitochondria undergo DRP1-mediated fission in constricted cytoplasmic regions caused by cell adhesion to uneven surfaces.
evidence: Concluded from vinyl disk experiments showing DRP1-dependent fission at constricted regions.

claim: ER tubules mark mitochondrial fission sites in unstimulated conditions.
source: In unstimulated conditions, ER tubules mark mitochondrial fission sites (Friedman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Friedman et al., 2011.

claim: The ER wraps around and constricts mitochondria prior to fission, likely by locally polymerizing actin via the activities of INF2 and Spire1C.
source: It has thus been proposed that the ER wraps around and constricts mitochondria prior to fission, likely by locally polymerizing actin via the activities of INverted Formin 2 (INF2) (Korobova et al., 2013) and Spire1C (Manor et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korobova et al., 2013 and Manor et al., 2015.

claim: The tip-mediated indentation of cells pushed the ER away from the site of force application and subsequent mitochondrial fission.
source: However, when performing AFM stimulation of U2OS cells stably expressing both a mitochondrial (mtBFP) and an ER (GFP-Sec61β) fluorescent marker, we observed that the tip-mediated indentation of cells pushed the ER away from the site of force application and subsequent mitochondrial fission (Figure 4A, Video 11).
evidence: Observed in AFM experiments shown in Figure 4A and Video 11.

claim: Mitochondria underwent fission when spanning over the edge of the groove whether or not the ER had been converted to sheets at the site of fission.
source: Mitochondria underwent fission when spanning over the edge of the groove whether or not the ER had been converted to sheets at the site of fission.
evidence: Observed in CLIMP-63 overexpression experiments.

claim: Some fission events occurred in areas with only ER sheets or without ER at all.
source: Some of these fission events occurred in areas with only ER sheets (Figure 4B, Video 12) or without ER at all (Figure 4C, Video 13).
evidence: Observed in experiments with ER morphology perturbations shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: 89% and 86% of the cells overexpressing ATL1-K80A and CLIMP-63, respectively, displayed a complete separation of their mitochondrial network.
source: Using the same metrics as in Figure 3D, we observed that 89% and 86% of the cells overexpressing ATL1-K80A and CLIMP-63, respectively, displayed a complete separation of their mitochondrial network.
evidence: Quantified from experiments with ER morphology perturbations.

claim: While the ER might have a function in force-induced fission, this function does not appear strictly necessary.
source: Thus, while the ER might have a function in force-induced fission, this function does not appear strictly necessary.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing fission can occur without ER involvement.

claim: Knocking-down the ER-associated isoform of INF2 did not have a visible effect on collision-induced fission in Shigella-infected cells.
source: Knocking-down the ER-associated isoform of INF2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) did not have a visible effect on collision-induced fission in Shigella-infected cells (Video 15)
evidence: Observed in INF2 knockdown experiments shown in Video 15.

claim: Of the 32 collisions observed in INF2-deficient cells, 25 led to a fission event, a proportion that is in line with that observed in scrambled siRNA-treated cells.
source: Indeed, of the 32 collisions observed in INF2-deficient cells, 25 led to a fission event, a proportion that is in line with that observed in scrambled siRNA-treated cells.
evidence: Quantified from INF2 knockdown experiments.

claim: 83% of the cells grown on gramophone records and showing a constricted cytoplasm had separated mitochondrial populations (n = 35) in INF2-depleted conditions.
source: Similarly, 83% of the cells grown on gramophone records and showing a constricted cytoplasm had separated mitochondrial populations (n = 35), again comparable to what we have observed in control cells.
evidence: Quantified from vinyl disk experiments with INF2 depletion, n=35.

claim: The INF2-mediated pathway does not play essential roles in mechanically induced fission.
source: These results suggest that the INF2-mediated pathway does not play essential roles in mechanically induced fission.
evidence: Concluded from INF2 knockdown experiments showing no significant effect on mechanically induced fission.

claim: The proportion of mechanically-induced mitochondrial fission in cytochalasin D-treated cells was similar to untreated cells (16 fission events from 17 touchdowns).
source: In these conditions, the proportion of mechanically-induced mitochondrial fission was similar to untreated cells (16 fission events from 17 touchdowns, Figure 4F, Video 16).
evidence: Quantified from AFM experiments with cytochalasin D treatment shown in Figure 4F and Video 16.

claim: Actin polymerization does not appear to be a necessary step in force-induced fission.
source: Thus, actin polymerization does not appear to be a necessary step in force-induced fission.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing fission occurs even when actin is disrupted by cytochalasin D.

claim: DRP1 is recruited to mitochondria by integral mitochondrial membrane adaptor molecules such as MFF and Mid49/51.
source: DRP1 is a cytosolic protein, and is recruited to mitochondria by integral mitochondrial membrane adaptor molecules such as mitochondrial fission factor (MFF) (Gandre-Babbe and van der Bliek, 2008) and mitochondrial dynamic protein of 49/51 kDa (Mid49/51) (Palmer et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gandre-Babbe and van der Bliek, 2008; Palmer et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011.

claim: MFF accumulates on dotted structures on mitochondria independently of the presence of DRP1.
source: MFF, for instance, accumulates on dotted structures on mitochondria independently of the presence of DRP1 (Otera et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Otera et al., 2010.

claim: MFF localized to foci irrespective of the presence of DRP1.
source: As previously reported (Otera et al., 2010), MFF localized to foci irrespective of the presence of DRP1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, consistent with prior report.

claim: MFF had a tendency to accumulate at constrictions that happen sporadically on non-perturbed mitochondrial tubule.
source: Additionally, we observed that MFF had a tendency to accumulate at constrictions that happen sporadically on non-perturbed mitochondrial tubule (Figure 5A, arrowheads in right panels).
evidence: Observed in experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the majority of the cases where mitochondria were visibly constricted on vinyl records, MFF foci were observed right on or at the edge of constrictions.
source: In the majority of the cases where mitochondria were visibly constricted, we observed MFF foci right on or at the edge of constrictions (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Observed in vinyl disk experiments shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MFF senses mechanical constrictions on mitochondria upstream of DRP1.
source: In the majority of the cases where mitochondria were visibly constricted, we observed MFF foci right on or at the edge of constrictions (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that MFF senses mechanical constrictions on mitochondria upstream of DRP1.
evidence: Inferred from observations of MFF localization to constricted sites in DRP1-depleted cells.

claim: Significantly fewer fission events were observed in MFF-deficient cells as compared to wild-type cells using the Shigella model (5.0% vs 56.5%, p<10−4).
source: In line with these observations, we observed significantly fewer fission events in MFF-deficient cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) as compared to wild-type cells using the Shigella as well as the vinyl disk models (5.0% vs 56.5% and 38% vs 80%, respectively; p<10−4 and p<10−9 from Fisher's exact tests, respectively).
evidence: Quantified from experiments with MFF depletion with statistical significance p<10^-4.

claim: Significantly fewer fission events were observed in MFF-deficient cells as compared to wild-type cells using the vinyl disk model (38% vs 80%, p<10−9).
source: In line with these observations, we observed significantly fewer fission events in MFF-deficient cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) as compared to wild-type cells using the Shigella as well as the vinyl disk models (5.0% vs 56.5% and 38% vs 80%, respectively; p<10−4 and p<10−9 from Fisher's exact tests, respectively).
evidence: Quantified from experiments with MFF depletion with statistical significance p<10^-9.

claim: GFP-MFF was recruited to constricted mitochondria in both Shigella and vinyl disk model systems.
source: GFP-MFF was recruited to constricted mitochondria in both model systems (Figure 5C–D, arrowheads, Video 17; Figure 5E–F).
evidence: Observed in live cell imaging experiments shown in Figures 5C-F and Video 17.

claim: MFF shows preferential accumulation on thinned mitochondria and could serve as a mechano-sensor for the recruitment of the fission machinery.
source: Thus, MFF shows preferential accumulation on thinned mitochondria and could therefore, serve as a mechano-sensor for the recruitment of the fission machinery.
evidence: Concluded from observations of MFF localization to constricted mitochondria.

claim: MFF acts not only as a sensor but also as an inducer of constrictions.
source: We also observe that MFF acts not only as a sensor but also as an inducer of constrictions.
evidence: Observed from experiments showing MFF can stabilize thin mitochondrial sections when overexpressed.

claim: MFF-stabilized thin, matrix-negative tubules were only observed when GFP-MFF was overexpressed to relatively high levels.
source: Importantly, these structures were only observed when GFP-MFF was overexpressed to relatively high levels, indicating that they resulted directly or indirectly from this overexpression.
evidence: Observed in experiments with varying levels of GFP-MFF expression.

claim: A protein with an affinity for constricted mitochondria will rapidly accumulate at constricted sites.
source: As shown by our Monte-Carlo simulations, a protein with increased affinity for mitochondria of reduced diameter will rapidly accumulate at constricted sites.
evidence: Demonstrated through Monte Carlo computer simulations.

claim: At high concentrations, a protein with affinity for constricted mitochondria will induce and stabilize constrictions.
source: At high concentrations however, it will induce and stabilize constrictions, two behaviors that mimic what we observe for GFP-MFF in live cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through Monte Carlo computer simulations and comparison to experimental observations.

claim: The propensity of a protein to localize to constricted sites is intrinsically coupled to its ability to stabilize constrictions.
source: Therefore, the propensity of a protein to localize to constricted sites is intrinsically coupled to its ability to stabilize constrictions.
evidence: Concluded from Monte Carlo simulations showing both behaviors emerge from the same property.

claim: The difference between the inducing and sensing behaviors of MFF seems to lie in the quantity of the protein.
source: The difference between the inducing and sensing behaviors seems to lie in the quantity of the protein.
evidence: Inferred from observations that MFF only stabilized constrictions when highly overexpressed.

claim: Sensing and inducing constrictions are two sides of the same coin, and the difference between sensing and inducing lies in the expression level of the factor.
source: Our simulations however highlight that sensing and inducing constrictions are two sides of the same coin, and that the difference between sensing and inducing lies in the expression level of the factor.
evidence: Concluded from Monte Carlo simulations and experimental observations.

claim: Mitochondria do not only respond to biochemical, but also to mechanical cues.
source: Our study shows that mitochondria do not only respond to biochemical, but also to mechanical cues
evidence: Concluded from multiple experimental approaches showing mechanical force triggers fission.

claim: Mechanical force, via the deformation of mitochondrial membranes, leads to mitochondrial fission, coupling a mechanical trigger to a biochemical response.
source: mechanical force, via the deformation of mitochondrial membranes, leads to mitochondrial fission, coupling a mechanical trigger to a biochemical response.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing mechanical stimulation leads to DRP1-mediated fission.

claim: Physical constriction might reduce mitochondrial diameter, causing MFF accumulation, subsequent DRP1 recruitment and mitochondrial fission.
source: Thus, a straightforward model for force-induced fission is that physical constriction might reduce mitochondrial diameter, causing MFF accumulation, subsequent DRP1 recruitment and mitochondrial fission.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental observations of MFF localization and DRP1 recruitment.

claim: In unperturbed adherent cells, mitochondria fission happens almost exclusively at sites in contact with the ER.
source: In unperturbed adherent cells, mitochondria fission happens almost exclusively at sites in contact with the ER (Friedman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Friedman et al., 2011.

claim: Mitochondrial tubules are generally larger in diameter (~500–700 nm) than the thickness of the cytoplasm in peripheral regions of adherent cells.
source: Mitochondrial tubules are generally larger in diameter (~500–700 nm) (Youle and Karbowski, 2005) than the thickness of the cytoplasm in these peripheral regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Youle and Karbowski, 2005.

claim: Super-resolution imaging studies show that peripheral mitochondria are flattened by the proximity of the 'ventral' and 'dorsal' actin cortices.
source: Indeed, super-resolution imaging studies show that peripheral mitochondria are flattened by the proximity of the 'ventral' and 'dorsal' actin cortices (Huang et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 2008 and Huang et al., 2016.

claim: Peripheral mitochondria adopt an elliptic – rather than tubular – cross-section, and slightly bulge from the cell surface.
source: adopt an elliptic – rather than tubular – cross-section, and slightly bulge from the cell surface (Wojcik et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wojcik et al., 2015.

claim: In live-cell high-speed AFM experiments, mitochondria are seen to deform the plasma membrane and underlying actin cytoskeleton by ~ 50 nm.
source: In live-cell high-speed AFM experiments, mitochondria are seen to deform the plasma membrane and underlying actin cytoskeleton by ~ 50 nm (Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2015.

claim: Peripheral mitochondria, sandwiched between the 'dorsal' and 'ventral' actin cortices, are mechanically constrained in these areas.
source: It is therefore clear that peripheral mitochondria, sandwiched between the 'dorsal' and 'ventral' actin cortices, are mechanically constrained in these areas.
evidence: Inferred from observations of mitochondrial flattening and deformation in peripheral regions.

claim: Crossing-over ER tubules, rigidified by an INF2- and Spire1C- mediated actin shell, might impose localized mechanical force to underlying mitochondria, triggering fission at ER-mitochondria encounter sites.
source: In this context, it is tempting to speculate that crossing-over ER tubules, rigidified by an INF2- and Spire1C- mediated actin shell, might impose localized mechanical force to underlying mitochondria, triggering fission at ER-mitochondria encounter sites.
evidence: Speculative model proposed to explain ER-mediated fission based on mechanical force hypothesis.

claim: The ER constitutes an intrinsic source of mechanical force for mitochondrial fission.
source: An appealing hypothesis is that the ER constitutes an intrinsic source of mechanical force.
evidence: Hypothesized based on observations that ER is dispensable when extrinsic mechanical force is applied.

claim: For ER-mediated fission events, the ER may be imposing force rather than providing biochemical signals.
source: This, in turn, suggests that for ER-mediated fission events, the ER may be imposing force rather than providing biochemical signals.
evidence: Speculated based on observations that ER is not strictly necessary when mechanical force is applied externally.

claim: The mechanical force model might explain why actin is necessary for mitochondrial fission, unless cells are mechanically stimulated with an AFM.
source: Because actin is an important force-generator in the cell, our model might also explain why it is necessary for mitochondrial fission (Korobova et al., 2013; Manor et al., 2015), unless cells are mechanically stimulated with an AFM (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: Proposed explanation based on actin's role as force generator and observations that actin is dispensable with AFM stimulation.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion and fission have been proposed to serve in the repair of damaged mitochondria by fusing with healthy ones.
source: Both processes have been proposed to serve in the repair of damaged mitochondria by fusing with healthy ones
evidence: Established hypothesis in the field about mitochondrial dynamics functions.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion and fission have been proposed to serve in the segregation of terminally damaged mitochondria for disposal by mitophagy.
source: in the segregation of terminally damaged mitochondria for disposal by mitophagy
evidence: Established hypothesis in the field about mitochondrial dynamics functions, supported by citation to Twig et al., 2008.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion and fission have been proposed to serve in the correct apportionment of mitochondria to daughter cells upon mitosis.
source: and in the correct apportionment of mitochondria to daughter cells upon mitosis (Katajisto et al., 2015; Twig et al., 2008).
evidence: Established hypothesis in the field about mitochondrial dynamics functions, supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondria undergo DRP1- and MFF-mediated fission in response to mechanical stimulation.
source: Here, we show that mitochondria undergo DRP1- and MFF-mediated fission in response to mechanical stimulation.
evidence: Main finding of the study demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches.

claim: By resolving any resulting mechanical strain, fission might enable mitochondria to escape shearing and ripping, and avoid entanglements.
source: By resolving any resulting mechanical strain, fission might enable mitochondria to escape shearing and ripping, (which could lead to Cytochrome-C release and apoptotic cell death), and avoid entanglements.
evidence: Proposed functional significance of mechanically-induced fission based on experimental findings.

claim: DRP1 activity may be paralleled to that of topoisomerase-II in disentangling the genome.
source: In that capacity, DRP1 activity may be paralleled to that of topoisomerase-II in disentangling the genome.
evidence: Analogy proposed to explain the function of DRP1 in resolving mitochondrial entanglements.

claim: Concatenations between mitochondria and the ER are observed in mammalian cells using serial block-face scanning electron microscopy.
source: Using serial block-face scanning electron microscopy, we observe concatenations between mitochondria and the ER in mammalian cells (our unpublished observations).
evidence: Observed through electron microscopy, though unpublished at time of manuscript.

claim: Entanglements between mitochondria and ER are likely to induce mechanical strain on mitochondria, leading to their resolution by fission.
source: Given the dynamic nature of these organelles, entanglements are likely to induce mechanical strain on mitochondria, therefore leading to their resolution by fission.
evidence: Inferred from observations of concatenations and the mechanical fission mechanism.

claim: Mitochondrial fission is the prime mechanism to resolve concatenations between mitochondria and ER.
source: Unlike mitochondrial fission, ER fission is not frequently observed. Thus, we presume that mitochondrial fission is the prime mechanism to resolve these concatenations.
evidence: Inferred from the relative frequency of mitochondrial vs ER fission events.

claim: Mechano-induced mitochondrial remodeling could play particularly important roles during cell migration through narrow passages, such as leukocyte extravasation and immune surveillance.
source: Mechano-induced mitochondrial remodeling could play particularly important roles during cell migration through narrow passages, such as leukocyte extravasation and immune surveillance (Muller, 2011; Nourshargh and Alon, 2014)
evidence: Speculated physiological relevance supported by citations about cell migration.

claim: Mechano-induced mitochondrial remodeling could play particularly important roles during cancer cell metastasis.
source: Mechano-induced mitochondrial remodeling could play particularly important roles during cell migration through narrow passages, such as leukocyte extravasation and immune surveillance (Muller, 2011; Nourshargh and Alon, 2014) as well as cancer cell metastasis (Friedl and Wolf, 2003).
evidence: Speculated physiological relevance supported by citation about cancer cell migration.

claim: Mechanical force can be coupled to a biochemical process crucial for intracellular membrane shaping and distribution.
source: In conclusion, our study shows that mechanical force can be coupled to a biochemical process crucial for intracellular membrane shaping and distribution, providing a new perspective in mitochondrial dynamics and organelle interactions.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental findings.

claim: Mitochondrial fission is triggered by mechanical forces.
source: Here, we show that mitochondrial fission is triggered by mechanical forces.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Mechano-stimulation of mitochondria via encounter with motile intracellular pathogens results in the recruitment of the mitochondrial fission machinery, and subsequent division.
source: Mechano-stimulation of mitochondria – via encounter with motile intracellular pathogens, via external pressure applied by an atomic force microscope, or via cell migration across uneven microsurfaces – results in the recruitment of the mitochondrial fission machinery, and subsequent division.
evidence: Demonstrated through Shigella infection experiments showing DRP1 recruitment and fission.

claim: Mechano-stimulation of mitochondria via external pressure applied by an atomic force microscope results in the recruitment of the mitochondrial fission machinery, and subsequent division.
source: Mechano-stimulation of mitochondria – via encounter with motile intracellular pathogens, via external pressure applied by an atomic force microscope, or via cell migration across uneven microsurfaces – results in the recruitment of the mitochondrial fission machinery, and subsequent division.
evidence: Demonstrated through AFM experiments showing force-induced fission.

claim: Mechano-stimulation of mitochondria via cell migration across uneven microsurfaces results in the recruitment of the mitochondrial fission machinery, and subsequent division.
source: Mechano-stimulation of mitochondria – via encounter with motile intracellular pathogens, via external pressure applied by an atomic force microscope, or via cell migration across uneven microsurfaces – results in the recruitment of the mitochondrial fission machinery, and subsequent division.
evidence: Demonstrated through vinyl disk experiments showing fission at constricted regions.

claim: MFF, owing to affinity for narrow mitochondria, acts as a membrane-bound force sensor to recruit the fission machinery to mechanically strained sites.
source: We propose that MFF, owing to affinity for narrow mitochondria, acts as a membrane-bound force sensor to recruit the fission machinery to mechanically strained sites.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on observations of MFF localization to constricted mitochondria.

claim: Mitochondria adapt to the environment by sensing and responding to biomechanical cues.
source: Thus, mitochondria adapt to the environment by sensing and responding to biomechanical cues.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing mitochondria undergo fission in response to mechanical stimulation.

claim: Mechanical triggers can be coupled to biochemical responses in membrane dynamics.
source: Our findings that mechanical triggers can be coupled to biochemical responses in membrane dynamics may explain how organelles orderly cohabit in the crowded cytoplasm.
evidence: Proposed broader implication of the findings for understanding organelle organization.
